claim: CD73 is an ectonucleotidase overexpressed on tumor cells that suppresses anti-tumor immunity.
source: CD73 is an ectonucleotidase overexpressed on tumor cells that suppresses anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about CD73's role in cancer.

claim: Several CD73 inhibitors are currently being evaluated in the clinic, including in large randomized clinical trials.
source: Accordingly, several CD73 inhibitors are currently being evaluated in the clinic, including in large randomized clinical trials.
evidence: This statement references ongoing clinical trials as factual information.

claim: CD73 significantly enhances tumor cell mitochondrial respiration.
source: Using metabolomics, we discovered that CD73 significantly enhances tumor cell mitochondrial respiration and aspartate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by metabolomics data.

claim: CD73 significantly enhances tumor cell aspartate biosynthesis.
source: Using metabolomics, we discovered that CD73 significantly enhances tumor cell mitochondrial respiration and aspartate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Rescuing aspartate biosynthesis was sufficient to restore proliferation of CD73-deficient tumors in immune deficient mice.
source: Importantly, rescuing aspartate biosynthesis was sufficient to restore proliferation of CD73-deficient tumors in immune deficient mice.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding from in vivo studies in NRG mice.

claim: CD73 enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) in a large panel of mouse and human tumor cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of a large panel of mouse and human tumor cells demonstrated that CD73 enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolytic reserve.
evidence: This finding is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data across multiple cell lines.

claim: CD73 enhanced glycolytic reserve in a large panel of mouse and human tumor cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of a large panel of mouse and human tumor cells demonstrated that CD73 enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolytic reserve.
evidence: This finding is supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analysis data across multiple cell lines.

claim: Targeting CD73 decreased tumor cell metabolic fitness.
source: Targeting CD73 decreased tumor cell metabolic fitness, increased genomic instability and suppressed poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Targeting CD73 increased genomic instability.
source: Targeting CD73 decreased tumor cell metabolic fitness, increased genomic instability and suppressed poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) activity.
evidence: This is supported by γH2AX foci analysis showing increased DNA damage in CD73-deficient cells.

claim: Targeting CD73 suppressed poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) activity.
source: Targeting CD73 decreased tumor cell metabolic fitness, increased genomic instability and suppressed poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) activity.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis showing reduced PARylation levels in CD73-deficient cells.

claim: CD73 catalyzes the phosphohydrolysis of adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
source: CD73 is an ectonucleotidase that catalyzes the phosphohydrolysis of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), thus contributing to the breakdown of pro-inflammatory adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into immunosuppressive ADO.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about CD73's enzymatic function.

claim: CD73 contributes to the breakdown of pro-inflammatory adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into immunosuppressive adenosine.
source: CD73 is an ectonucleotidase that catalyzes the phosphohydrolysis of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), thus contributing to the breakdown of pro-inflammatory adenosine triphosphate (ATP) into immunosuppressive ADO.
evidence: This describes the established role of CD73 in the adenosine pathway.

claim: Accumulation of extracellular adenosine in the tumor microenvironment favors cancer progression.
source: Accumulation of extracellular ADO in the tumor microenvironment favors cancer progression by activating ADO specific G-coupled protein receptors (GPCRs) expressed on immune cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts and tumor cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adenosine's role in cancer.

claim: High affinity A2A and low affinity A2B receptors elevate intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels.
source: Of the four ADO receptors, high affinity A2A and low affinity A2B receptors elevate intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels and contribute to suppress immune cell function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adenosine receptor signaling.

claim: A2A and A2B receptors contribute to suppress immune cell function.
source: Of the four ADO receptors, high affinity A2A and low affinity A2B receptors elevate intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels and contribute to suppress immune cell function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adenosine receptor function in immunity.

claim: In triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes.
source: In human cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) and ovarian cancer, CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes, impaired tumor immune surveillance and resistance to chemotherapy (Loi et al., 2013; Bareche et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical studies.

claim: In ovarian cancer, CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes.
source: In human cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) and ovarian cancer, CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes, impaired tumor immune surveillance and resistance to chemotherapy (Loi et al., 2013; Bareche et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical studies.

claim: CD73 expression is associated with impaired tumor immune surveillance.
source: In human cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) and ovarian cancer, CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes, impaired tumor immune surveillance and resistance to chemotherapy (Loi et al., 2013; Bareche et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: CD73 expression is associated with resistance to chemotherapy.
source: In human cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) and ovarian cancer, CD73 expression is generally associated with poor clinical outcomes, impaired tumor immune surveillance and resistance to chemotherapy (Loi et al., 2013; Bareche et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Potent and selective CD73 inhibitors have recently been developed.
source: Potent and selective CD73 inhibitors have recently been developed and are now being evaluated in randomized clinical trials with encouraging preliminary results reported in lung cancer and pancreatic cancer patients (Allard et al., 2020; Augustin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited references to clinical development.

claim: CD73 inhibitors are being evaluated in randomized clinical trials with encouraging preliminary results in lung cancer patients.
source: Potent and selective CD73 inhibitors have recently been developed and are now being evaluated in randomized clinical trials with encouraging preliminary results reported in lung cancer and pancreatic cancer patients (Allard et al., 2020; Augustin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical trial reports.

claim: CD73 inhibitors are being evaluated in randomized clinical trials with encouraging preliminary results in pancreatic cancer patients.
source: Potent and selective CD73 inhibitors have recently been developed and are now being evaluated in randomized clinical trials with encouraging preliminary results reported in lung cancer and pancreatic cancer patients (Allard et al., 2020; Augustin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical trial reports.

claim: Targeting CD73 can inhibit human tumor xenografts in severely immunocompromised mice.
source: While CD73 inhibitors can stimulate anti-tumor immunity, early studies reported that targeting CD73 can also inhibit human tumor xenografts in severely immunocompromised mice (Zhou et al., 2007; Zhi et al., 2007; Zhi et al., 2010; Rust et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies in immunocompromised mouse models.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CD73 has been observed to increase the sensitivity of CD73-expressing tumor cells to cytotoxic drugs in vitro.
source: Moreover, pharmacological inhibition or gene-deletion of CD73 has also been observed to increase the sensitivity of CD73-expressing tumor cells to cytotoxic drugs in vitro (Loi et al., 2013; Ujházy et al., 1996; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited in vitro studies.

claim: Gene-deletion of CD73 has been observed to increase the sensitivity of CD73-expressing tumor cells to cytotoxic drugs in vitro.
source: Moreover, pharmacological inhibition or gene-deletion of CD73 has also been observed to increase the sensitivity of CD73-expressing tumor cells to cytotoxic drugs in vitro (Loi et al., 2013; Ujházy et al., 1996; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited in vitro studies.

claim: Activation of pro-survival pathways downstream of A2B receptors has been proposed to explain immune-independent effects of CD73.
source: Although activation of pro-survival pathways downstream of A2B receptors has been proposed to explain immune-independent effects of CD73, alternative hypotheses have not been explored (Mittal et al., 2016; Lan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Rewiring of cancer cells' metabolism is central to their adaptation to hostile tumor microenvironments.
source: Rewiring of cancer cells' metabolism is central to their adaptation to hostile tumor microenvironments (Zhi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer metabolism supported by citation.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration has been shown to be critical for proliferating cells.
source: While cancer cells can shift their metabolism from highly efficient ATP-producing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to low ATP-yielding glycolysis despite presence of oxygen (e.g. Warburg effect), mitochondrial respiration has been shown to be critical for proliferating cells and for maintaining tumor cells invasiveness, metabolic adaptation, chemoresistance and stemness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of mitochondrial respiration in cancer.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is critical for maintaining tumor cells invasiveness, metabolic adaptation, chemoresistance and stemness.
source: While cancer cells can shift their metabolism from highly efficient ATP-producing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to low ATP-yielding glycolysis despite presence of oxygen (e.g. Warburg effect), mitochondrial respiration has been shown to be critical for proliferating cells and for maintaining tumor cells invasiveness, metabolic adaptation, chemoresistance and stemness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial respiration in cancer.

claim: Tumor cells often require respiration for survival.
source: Accordingly, tumor cells are not only capable of respiration but often require respiration for survival (Ashton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: In proliferating cells, mitochondrial respiration provides electron acceptors to support biosynthesis of aspartate.
source: In proliferating cells, mitochondrial respiration provides electron acceptors to support biosynthesis of aspartate, an indispensable amino acid for nucleotide and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of mitochondrial respiration in aspartate biosynthesis.

claim: Aspartate is an indispensable amino acid for nucleotide and protein synthesis.
source: In proliferating cells, mitochondrial respiration provides electron acceptors to support biosynthesis of aspartate, an indispensable amino acid for nucleotide and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration requires nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) in its oxidized and reduced forms to allow movement of electrons through the electron transport chain (ETC).
source: Mitochondrial respiration requires nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) in its oxidized and reduced forms to allow movement of electrons through the electron transport chain (ETC).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about mitochondrial respiration.

claim: NAD is an important co-substrate for poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs).
source: In addition of supporting respiration, NAD is also an important co-substrate for many enzymes, notably poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs) that play a central role in genomic stability by catalyzing the addition of poly-ADP-ribose to proteins (also known as PARylation; Wei and Yu, 2016; Pommier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PARPs play a central role in genomic stability by catalyzing the addition of poly-ADP-ribose to proteins.
source: In addition of supporting respiration, NAD is also an important co-substrate for many enzymes, notably poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs) that play a central role in genomic stability by catalyzing the addition of poly-ADP-ribose to proteins (also known as PARylation; Wei and Yu, 2016; Pommier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PARP function supported by citations.

claim: Intracellular NAD levels are maintained by de novo synthesis from L-tryptophan (Trp).
source: Intracellular NAD levels are maintained either by de novo synthesis from L-tryptophan (Trp), or by more effective salvage pathways that recycle NAD from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), or nicotinamide riboside (NR) (Verdin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAD biosynthesis supported by citation.

claim: Intracellular NAD levels are maintained by salvage pathways that recycle NAD from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), or nicotinamide riboside (NR).
source: Intracellular NAD levels are maintained either by de novo synthesis from L-tryptophan (Trp), or by more effective salvage pathways that recycle NAD from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), or nicotinamide riboside (NR) (Verdin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAD biosynthesis supported by citation.

claim: Extracellular NMN is dephosphorylated to NR before cellular internalization by equilibrative nucleotide transporters (ENTs).
source: Extracellular NMN is dephosphorylated to NR before cellular internalization by equilibrative nucleotide transporters (ENTs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMN/NR metabolism.

claim: Intracellular NR is re-phosphorylated by NRK1 into NMN.
source: Intracellular NR is then re-phosphorylated by NRK1 into NMN, a substrate for adenylyl transferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Katsyuba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAD biosynthesis supported by citations.

claim: NMN is a substrate for adenylyl transferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD.
source: Intracellular NR is then re-phosphorylated by NRK1 into NMN, a substrate for adenylyl transferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Katsyuba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAD biosynthesis supported by citations.

claim: NMN can be generated from intracellular or extracellular NAM via the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT.
source: NMN can also be generated from intracellular or extracellular NAM via the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT (Katsyuba et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAD biosynthesis supported by citation.

claim: Some studies have suggested a role for CD73 in NAD synthesis from extracellular NR.
source: Interestingly, some studies have suggested a role for CD73 in NAD synthesis from extracellular NR (Garavaglia et al., 2012; Mateuszuk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: CD73 deletion in MDA-MB-231 human triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells significantly delayed tumor growth in severely immunodeficient Nod-Rag-gamma (NRG) mice.
source: Consistent with prior work (Rust et al., 2013) and in support of immune-independent effects, CD73 deletion in MDA-MB-231 human triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells significantly delayed tumor growth in severely immunodeficient Nod-Rag-gamma (NRG) mice, which lack T cells, B cells, NK cells and functional macrophages (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vivo tumor growth studies shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NRG mice lack T cells, B cells, NK cells and functional macrophages.
source: Consistent with prior work (Rust et al., 2013) and in support of immune-independent effects, CD73 deletion in MDA-MB-231 human triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells significantly delayed tumor growth in severely immunodeficient Nod-Rag-gamma (NRG) mice, which lack T cells, B cells, NK cells and functional macrophages (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NRG mouse model.

claim: NT5E gene deletion had no impact on MDA-MB-231 cell proliferation in standard cell culture conditions (25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine).
source: While NT5E (gene encoding for CD73) gene deletion had no impact in standard cell culture conditions (i.e. 25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine), it significantly suppressed cell proliferation and viability in nutrients-limiting conditions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite no difference in cellular uptake of glucose or glutamine, as shown using a fluorescent glucose analog (i.e. 2-NDBG; Figure 1C) and by measurements of glutamine depletion in media (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from in vitro proliferation assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NT5E gene deletion significantly suppressed MDA-MB-231 cell proliferation in nutrients-limiting conditions.
source: While NT5E (gene encoding for CD73) gene deletion had no impact in standard cell culture conditions (i.e. 25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine), it significantly suppressed cell proliferation and viability in nutrients-limiting conditions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite no difference in cellular uptake of glucose or glutamine, as shown using a fluorescent glucose analog (i.e. 2-NDBG; Figure 1C) and by measurements of glutamine depletion in media (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from in vitro proliferation assays shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NT5E gene deletion significantly suppressed MDA-MB-231 cell viability in nutrients-limiting conditions.
source: While NT5E (gene encoding for CD73) gene deletion had no impact in standard cell culture conditions (i.e. 25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine), it significantly suppressed cell proliferation and viability in nutrients-limiting conditions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite no difference in cellular uptake of glucose or glutamine, as shown using a fluorescent glucose analog (i.e. 2-NDBG; Figure 1C) and by measurements of glutamine depletion in media (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from viability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no difference in cellular uptake of glucose between CD73-positive and CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: While NT5E (gene encoding for CD73) gene deletion had no impact in standard cell culture conditions (i.e. 25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine), it significantly suppressed cell proliferation and viability in nutrients-limiting conditions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite no difference in cellular uptake of glucose or glutamine, as shown using a fluorescent glucose analog (i.e. 2-NDBG; Figure 1C) and by measurements of glutamine depletion in media (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from 2-NBDG uptake assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no difference in cellular uptake of glutamine between CD73-positive and CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: While NT5E (gene encoding for CD73) gene deletion had no impact in standard cell culture conditions (i.e. 25 mM glucose and 2 mM glutamine), it significantly suppressed cell proliferation and viability in nutrients-limiting conditions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), despite no difference in cellular uptake of glucose or glutamine, as shown using a fluorescent glucose analog (i.e. 2-NDBG; Figure 1C) and by measurements of glutamine depletion in media (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from glutamine depletion assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Aspartate biosynthesis from glucose was significantly reduced by nearly 50% in CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 tumor cells.
source: Strikingly, while the isopotomers distribution and relative abundance of most intermediate metabolites were unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), aspartate biosynthesis from glucose or glutamine (Figure 1E) was significantly reduced – by nearly 50% – in CD73neg tumor cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from stable isotope tracer analysis shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Aspartate biosynthesis from glutamine was significantly reduced by nearly 50% in CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 tumor cells.
source: Strikingly, while the isopotomers distribution and relative abundance of most intermediate metabolites were unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), aspartate biosynthesis from glucose or glutamine (Figure 1E) was significantly reduced – by nearly 50% – in CD73neg tumor cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from stable isotope tracer analysis shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells significantly increased intracellular aspartate levels.
source: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells indeed significantly increased intracellular aspartate levels (Figure 1H) and effectively restored proliferation of CD73neg MDA-MB-231 tumor cells, both in vitro in glutamine-restricted conditions (Figure 1I) and in vivo in immunodeficient NRG mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells effectively restored proliferation of CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 tumor cells in vitro in glutamine-restricted conditions.
source: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells indeed significantly increased intracellular aspartate levels (Figure 1H) and effectively restored proliferation of CD73neg MDA-MB-231 tumor cells, both in vitro in glutamine-restricted conditions (Figure 1I) and in vivo in immunodeficient NRG mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from in vitro proliferation assays shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells effectively restored proliferation of CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 tumor cells in vivo in immunodeficient NRG mice.
source: Asparagine treatment of gpASNase1-expressing cells indeed significantly increased intracellular aspartate levels (Figure 1H) and effectively restored proliferation of CD73neg MDA-MB-231 tumor cells, both in vitro in glutamine-restricted conditions (Figure 1I) and in vivo in immunodeficient NRG mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from in vivo tumor growth studies shown in Figure 1J.

claim: CD73-deficiency impaired tumor growth via impaired aspartate biosynthesis.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrated that CD73-deficiency impaired tumor growth via impaired aspartate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that rescuing aspartate biosynthesis restores tumor growth.

claim: Aspartate biosynthesis is an essential function of mitochondrial respiration.
source: Since aspartate biosynthesis is an essential function of mitochondrial respiration (Birsoy et al., 2015; Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2015), and that aspartate fuels OXPHOS (Cheng et al., 2018), we evaluated the impact of CD73 on mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aspartate fuels OXPHOS.
source: Since aspartate biosynthesis is an essential function of mitochondrial respiration (Birsoy et al., 2015; Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2015), and that aspartate fuels OXPHOS (Cheng et al., 2018), we evaluated the impact of CD73 on mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 cells displayed significantly reduced OXPHOS compared to CD73-positive cells in both glutamine replete and glutamine limiting conditions.
source: Strikingly, CD73neg MDA-MB-231 cells displayed significantly reduced OXPHOS (Figure 2B) and reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73pos cells in both glutamine replete and glutamine limiting conditions (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD73-negative MDA-MB-231 cells displayed reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73-positive cells in both glutamine replete and glutamine limiting conditions.
source: Strikingly, CD73neg MDA-MB-231 cells displayed significantly reduced OXPHOS (Figure 2B) and reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73pos cells in both glutamine replete and glutamine limiting conditions (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking CD73 with a neutralizing mAb significantly suppressed OXPHOS.
source: In addition, blocking CD73 with a neutralizing mAb (Häusler et al., 2014) also significantly suppressed OXPHOS and glycolytic reserve (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Blocking CD73 with a neutralizing mAb significantly suppressed glycolytic reserve.
source: In addition, blocking CD73 with a neutralizing mAb (Häusler et al., 2014) also significantly suppressed OXPHOS and glycolytic reserve (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Similar results on OXPHOS and glycolytic reserve were obtained in additional murine cell lines (4T1, SM1 LWT1).
source: Importantly, similar results were obtained in additional murine cell lines (4T1, SM1 LWT1), human cell lines (SK23MEL, PANC1, SKOV3, and HCC1954) and in primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) derived from CD73-deficient mice (Figure 2D–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 2D-H.

claim: Similar results on OXPHOS and glycolytic reserve were obtained in human cell lines (SK23MEL, PANC1, SKOV3, and HCC1954).
source: Importantly, similar results were obtained in additional murine cell lines (4T1, SM1 LWT1), human cell lines (SK23MEL, PANC1, SKOV3, and HCC1954) and in primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) derived from CD73-deficient mice (Figure 2D–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 2D-H.

claim: Similar results on OXPHOS and glycolytic reserve were obtained in primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) derived from CD73-deficient mice.
source: Importantly, similar results were obtained in additional murine cell lines (4T1, SM1 LWT1), human cell lines (SK23MEL, PANC1, SKOV3, and HCC1954) and in primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) derived from CD73-deficient mice (Figure 2D–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CD73-deficient tumor cells displayed reduced ratios of ATP to ADP.
source: Consistent with the observed defect in mitochondrial respiration, CD73 NT5E gene-targeted tumor cells also displayed reduced ratios of ATP to ADP or AMP (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CD73-deficient tumor cells displayed reduced ratios of ATP to AMP.
source: Consistent with the observed defect in mitochondrial respiration, CD73 NT5E gene-targeted tumor cells also displayed reduced ratios of ATP to ADP or AMP (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: No difference was observed in GOT1 and GOT2 mRNA expression between CD73-positive and CD73-negative cells.
source: However, no difference was observed in GOT1 and GOT2 mRNA expression, which encode enzymes that generate aspartate from oxaloacetate (Birsoy et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), or other tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle-related enzymes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from transcriptional analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: GOT1 and GOT2 encode enzymes that generate aspartate from oxaloacetate.
source: However, no difference was observed in GOT1 and GOT2 mRNA expression, which encode enzymes that generate aspartate from oxaloacetate (Birsoy et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), or other tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle-related enzymes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD73 is overexpressed in tumor-initiating cells (TIC) to promote stemness.
source: As CD73 is overexpressed in tumor-initiating cells (TIC) to promote stemness (Katsuta et al., 2016; Song et al., 2017), and that TIC rely on OXPHOS to support tumorigenesis (Snyder et al., 2018), we next evaluated the impact of CD73 on the metabolic fitness of putative TIC (ALDHHigh CD44+ CD24-) derived from MDA-MB-231 cell cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TIC rely on OXPHOS to support tumorigenesis.
source: As CD73 is overexpressed in tumor-initiating cells (TIC) to promote stemness (Katsuta et al., 2016; Song et al., 2017), and that TIC rely on OXPHOS to support tumorigenesis (Snyder et al., 2018), we next evaluated the impact of CD73 on the metabolic fitness of putative TIC (ALDHHigh CD44+ CD24-) derived from MDA-MB-231 cell cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD73-negative TIC displayed significantly suppressed OXPHOS compared to CD73-positive TIC.
source: Similar to the bulk culture, CD73neg TIC also displayed significantly suppressed OXPHOS and reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73pos TIC (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CD73-negative TIC displayed reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73-positive TIC.
source: Similar to the bulk culture, CD73neg TIC also displayed significantly suppressed OXPHOS and reduced glycolytic reserve compared to CD73pos TIC (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CD73 plays a critical role in promoting mitochondrial respiration in proliferating tumor cells.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrated that CD73 plays a critical role in promoting mitochondrial respiration in proliferating tumor cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data across multiple cell lines and conditions.

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells express A2A and A2B receptors.
source: MDA-MB-231 cells express A2A and A2B receptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; Fernandez-Gallardo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and cited literature.

claim: Treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Nevertheless, treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) or an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Treatment with an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Nevertheless, treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) or an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) had no effect on glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Nevertheless, treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) or an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Treatment with an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Nevertheless, treatment with an A2A antagonist (SCH58261) or an A2B antagonist (PSB1115) had no effect on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Depletion of extracellular adenosine with rhADA had no impact on mitochondrial respiration of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Depletion of extracellular ADO with rhADA (Figure 2J), or treatment with NECA (Figure 2K), also had no impact on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Depletion of extracellular adenosine with rhADA had no impact on glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Depletion of extracellular ADO with rhADA (Figure 2J), or treatment with NECA (Figure 2K), also had no impact on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Treatment with NECA had no impact on mitochondrial respiration of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Depletion of extracellular ADO with rhADA (Figure 2J), or treatment with NECA (Figure 2K), also had no impact on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Treatment with NECA had no impact on glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Depletion of extracellular ADO with rhADA (Figure 2J), or treatment with NECA (Figure 2K), also had no impact on mitochondrial respiration or glycolysis of MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Seahorse analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: CD73 promoted metabolic fitness independently of adenosine signaling.
source: Our results thus indicated that CD73 promoted metabolic fitness independently of ADO signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing no effect of adenosine receptor antagonists or adenosine depletion.

claim: NAD+ is a coenzyme that plays a central role in mitochondrial respiration.
source: NAD + is a coenzyme that plays a central role in mitochondrial respiration (Verdin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD73-deficient tumor cells displayed impaired maximal glycolytic capacity following oligomycin treatment.
